headline: A quiet beginning
development: The embryo is settling into the lining of the uterus and the neural tube — the future brain and spine — is starting to form. Two tiny layers of cells are already organizing into everything your baby will become.
momTips: If you haven't started a prenatal vitamin with folate yet, now is the moment — it matters most in these early weeks.
You may feel nothing at all yet — that's normal. The vitamin and the rest are already doing their job.
If the two lines still don't feel real, that's okay. There's no required way to feel this week.
Note the first day of your last period somewhere safe; your provider will ask.
Cutting back on caffeine starts gently — one small cup a day is generally considered fine.
partnerTips: Celebrate the news together in a small, private way — this is your shared secret for now.
She may look exactly the same and feel completely different — ask how she's doing, then really listen.
Take a quiet photo of these early days; you'll both want the 'before' someday.
Start learning the basics — what a due date means, what happens at the first appointment.
Keep the secret well; deciding who to tell, and when, is something to do together.

headline: First flickers
development: The heart is beginning to take shape and may pulse for the first time this week. The brain and spinal cord are forming from the neural tube.
momTips: Nausea can start now — keep plain crackers by the bed and eat something small before you get up.
Eat small and often; an empty stomach is nausea's best friend.
If smells suddenly ambush you, cold foods tend to smell less than hot ones.
Bloating and tender breasts are common this week — a softer bra is a real upgrade.
You don't have to announce anything yet; this week can belong to just the two of you.
partnerTips: Take over the cooking if smells start bothering her; an unscented kitchen is a real gift right now.
Keep crackers and water on her nightstand without being asked — mornings start rough.
If she's queasy, eat the fragrant takeout away from home for a while.
Ask 'what sounds edible today?' instead of 'what do you want for dinner?'
Read up on week five together — five minutes of knowing what's happening goes a long way.

headline: A heartbeat, almost
development: Little buds that will become arms and legs are appearing, and the heart is beating in a steady rhythm. Facial features — eyes and a tiny nose — are starting to form.
momTips: Fatigue is your body doing serious construction work; nap without guilt.
Ginger tea, ginger chews, or flat ginger ale — many find real relief in ginger.
Your blood volume is already rising; dizziness when standing quickly is common — rise slowly.
If you're calling providers this week, ask what their first-visit schedule looks like.
Guilt-free screen time and an early bedtime is a perfectly valid evening routine right now.
partnerTips: Handle the grocery run and stock up on whatever plain foods she's actually willing to eat.
Learn the difference between normal queasiness and not being able to keep fluids down — the second deserves a call.
Take on the litter box if you have a cat; it's hers to skip for the next nine months.
Keep dinner simple and smell-free; this is the season of plain pasta, and that's fine.
Tell her she's doing great even when all she did was lie on the couch — growing a human counts.

headline: Doubling by the day
development: Your baby has doubled in size since last week. Tiny hands and feet are emerging from paddle-shaped limbs, and the brain is growing by roughly a hundred cells a minute.
momTips: Sip water steadily through the day — dehydration makes nausea and headaches worse.
If nausea peaks around now, vitamin B6 is the most-studied option — ask your provider about it.
Your waist may thicken before any bump appears; leggings are your friend.
Frequent urination has begun — normal, and it will ease mid-pregnancy before returning.
Write down how this week felt; the details fade faster than you'd think.
partnerTips: Learn one new thing about this week of pregnancy and share it with her — it shows you're in it together.
Stock the fridge with her three safe foods and guard them like treasure.
Offer to make the first prenatal appointment call — phone admin is help too.
If she's exhausted by 7pm, run the bath, take the dishes, and let the evening be short.
Keep a shared note of questions for the provider so neither of you blanks at the appointment.

headline: Fingers and toes begin
development: Fingers and toes are forming, and the eyelids are starting to cover the eyes. Your baby is making small, spontaneous movements you can't feel yet.
momTips: If your first ultrasound is around now, bring tissues — seeing that flicker is surprisingly emotional.
Your provider may offer early bloodwork around now — it's routine, not a warning sign.
If mornings are hard, eat something small before your feet touch the floor.
A metallic taste is a real pregnancy thing; cold water with lemon can blunt it.
Rest when the tiredness comes — first-trimester fatigue is earned, not laziness.
partnerTips: Go with her to the first ultrasound if you possibly can; ask the questions she's too overwhelmed to ask.
Before the ultrasound, ask if there's anything she's nervous about — then just hold that with her.
Handle the scheduling and insurance calls if she'll let you; logistics are love.
Save that first ultrasound image somewhere backed up.
Keep the household running quietly this week — meals, laundry, trash — without keeping score.

headline: All essential parts
development: All the essential organs have begun to form, and the tail at the base of the spine is disappearing. Tiny earlobes and the tip of a nose are taking shape.
momTips: Your clothes may start feeling snug at the waist — a hair tie through the button loop is the classic trick.
Your waistband may be snug even without a visible bump — bloating is doing that, and it's normal.
If you're ravenous one hour and queasy the next, you're textbook. Small snacks bridge both.
Mood swings can arrive uninvited; naming them out loud takes away some of their power.
Start a simple folder for appointment notes and lab results — future you will be grateful.
partnerTips: Offer a back rub before bed; her body is working around the clock even while she sleeps.
Ask about her dreams — pregnancy dreams are famously vivid, and telling them helps.
Take over one weekly chore permanently, starting now. Pick the one she hates most.
If her favorite foods have betrayed her, quietly refresh the snack shelf with the new winners.
Learn this week's size comparison and use it — 'our blueberry' makes it real for both of you.

headline: Officially a fetus
development: This week the embryo graduates to fetus. Vital organs are formed and starting to function, and tiny nails are beginning to grow on fingers and toes.
momTips: If morning sickness is peaking, cold foods often smell less — try chilled fruit or yogurt.
If this is the worst of the nausea, relief often begins in the next few weeks — you're near the peak.
Veins may look more visible as blood volume climbs; it's your circulation doing its new job.
A prenatal vitamin that upsets your stomach can be swapped — ask for alternatives instead of quitting.
Round one of big decisions (screening tests) is coming; there's time to read before choosing.
partnerTips: Keep a running note on your phone of snacks she can tolerate, and keep them stocked.
Rub her shoulders before bed and don't make it a production — quiet care lands best.
If she's anxious about the upcoming screenings, offer to read the same article and compare notes.
Keep mornings slow where you can: make the tea, find the crackers, warm the car.
Notice how hard she's working at seeming normal; home should be the place she can stop.

headline: Hiccups and stretches
development: Your baby is stretching, somersaulting, and even hiccupping — all in secret. Tooth buds are forming beneath the gums, and the diaphragm is developing.
momTips: Consider scheduling any first-trimester screening tests your provider recommends this week.
Your uterus is now about grapefruit-sized; a little pelvic heaviness is expected.
If food aversions are running your life, protein hides well in smoothies and soups.
Skin changes — glow or breakouts, either is normal — come from the same hormone surge.
It's okay to start browsing maternity basics; soft waistbands help sooner than a real bump.
partnerTips: Start reading up on the screening options so the two of you can decide together, calmly.
Be the calm researcher: present options, not opinions, and let the decision be hers first.
If she's worried about telling work, role-play the conversation together.
Surprise her with the one snack that's been reliably safe all week.
Take a bump photo even if there's barely a bump — the series starts somewhere.

headline: Reflexes in rehearsal
development: Reflexes are kicking in — your baby's fingers can open and close, and the mouth makes sucking motions. The intestines are moving into place inside the abdomen.
momTips: Many parents share their news around now; there's no wrong time, only your time.
The risk of miscarriage drops meaningfully after this week — one reason many share now.
Dizziness can still visit; stand up slowly and keep snacks close.
If the nausea is loosening its grip, reintroduce the vegetables you abandoned — gently.
Your first-trimester screening window is open; ask your provider what's recommended for you.
partnerTips: If you're announcing soon, plan a reveal that feels like the two of you — not like anyone else's.
If you're telling family soon, agree on the order of phone calls — it prevents real hurt feelings.
Offer to be the one who tells the difficult-to-tell relative, if she wants that.
Celebrate the end of the first trimester's hardest stretch — plan something small and easy.
Keep a running list of name ideas you both like; it's early, and that's exactly the fun.

headline: Vocal cords, quietly
development: Vocal cords are forming, and your baby has tiny fingerprints on fingers the size of grains of rice. The placenta is fully up and running.
momTips: The second trimester is near — many people feel their energy return in the next few weeks.
As energy returns, gentle walks are a lovely way to feel like yourself again.
Round ligament twinges — quick, sharp, one-sided — often begin as the uterus grows.
Appetite may rebound with enthusiasm; keep protein-rich snacks within reach.
If you're still nauseous, you're not broken — for some it fades a few weeks later.
partnerTips: Notice and name the small wins: the first day without nausea is worth a toast (sparkling water counts).
Plan a tiny celebration for the second trimester — flowers and a nap both count.
Ask her what she missed most while feeling awful, then bring it back if it's safe.
Start the shared calendar for appointments; being there starts with knowing when they are.
Take her out for the meal she couldn't look at last month.

headline: The golden trimester
development: Welcome to the second trimester. Your baby can squint, frown, and may have started sucking a thumb. The kidneys are producing urine and the liver starts making bile.
momTips: With energy returning, gentle movement like walking or prenatal yoga can feel wonderful.
If round ligament pain surprises you, move slowly when rolling over or standing up.
Nasal congestion without a cold is a known pregnancy quirk — saline spray is a safe friend.
Your bump may begin to show now, or not for weeks — both timelines are normal.
Second-trimester appetite is real; aim it at protein and color when you can.
partnerTips: Plan a low-key date while energy is good — a walk, a breakfast out, an afternoon movie.
Book that easy date now — energy windows in pregnancy are worth scheduling around.
Tell her, out loud and specifically, how she's handling all of this.
Offer to research prenatal classes for later; having it on the radar calms everyone.
If she's ready to walk more, make the evening walk your shared ritual.

headline: Sensing the light
development: Though the eyes are still fused shut, your baby can sense light. The ears are nearly in their final position, and the skeleton is hardening from cartilage into bone.
momTips: Round ligament pain — a quick sharp tug on one side — is common now; move slowly when changing positions.
If your gums bleed when brushing, that's common — a soft brush helps, and mention it at your next dental visit.
You may feel hungrier at night; a small protein snack before bed steadies things.
Heartburn can start now — smaller meals and staying upright after eating help.
This is a good week to book the anatomy scan if your provider hasn't already.
partnerTips: Remind her that new aches are usually just stretching; a heating pad on low and your hand on her back help.
Warm a heating pad for her back before she asks; low heat only.
If new aches worry her, learn which ones are normal so you can reassure, not panic.
Offer a slow walk after dinner — it helps her digestion and your talking time.
Keep complimenting the bump specifically; she may be starting to feel self-conscious.

headline: Listening in
development: The ears are developed enough that your baby may begin to hear muted sounds — your heartbeat, your voice. The circulatory system is fully operational.
momTips: Talk or hum to your belly when it feels natural; your voice will be the most familiar sound in your baby's world.
If you haven't felt movement yet, that's completely normal — first flutters often wait until 18–22 weeks.
Congestion and nosebleeds can both appear now; a humidifier at night helps.
Your appetite may spike — keep a protein snack in your bag so hunger never catches you empty.
Back aching? Check your posture when sitting; a small cushion at the lower back works wonders.

Read aloud to the bump sometimes — it feels silly until it doesn't.
If she's showing now, tell her often how lovely she looks; mean it, say it plainly.
Take over the heavy lifting without commentary — groceries, laundry baskets, the litter box.
Plan the babymoon-ish weekend now if it's ever happening; the window is the next few months.

headline: Growing a layer of cozy
development: Your baby is starting to build a layer of fat beneath the skin, and the umbilical cord is getting thicker and stronger. Sweat glands are beginning to develop.
momTips: Sleep on your side with a pillow between your knees — it's kinder to your back and circulation.
Side sleeping becomes the recommendation from here on; the left side is the classic favorite.
Your center of gravity is shifting — expect the occasional clumsy day and go easy on yourself.
Vivid dreams are ramping up; keeping a notepad by the bed makes them fun instead of eerie.
If your appetite is back, iron-rich foods (lentils, lean beef, spinach) earn their place now.
partnerTips: If she's started shopping for a pregnancy pillow, surprise her by researching the good ones.
Give up the big pillow gracefully; her sleep arrangement now outranks yours.
If she wakes from strange dreams, listen to the whole plot — they're usually amazing.
Offer foot rubs on the regular; her circulation is working overtime.
Start noticing baby gear prices now so nothing shocks you later.

headline: Yawns in the dark
development: Your baby is yawning, stretching, and flexing those brand-new muscles. The nervous system is wiring up at astonishing speed, and myelin — the insulation around nerves — is starting to form.

You'll likely be asked about movement soon — those first flutters feel like bubbles or popcorn.
Posture matters more each week; stand tall, shoulders back, pelvis tucked slightly.
If back pain appears, a warm (not hot) compress on the lower back is the classic comfort.
Drink water before you feel thirsty; your blood volume is still climbing.

Clear your schedule for the anatomy scan day — work will survive without you.
Ask the sonographer your questions too; you're allowed to be amazed out loud.
Print one ultrasound photo for the fridge; small rituals make it real.
After the scan, take her to lunch and talk about what you both just saw.

headline: A waxy little coat
development: A protective, cheese-like coating called vernix is covering your baby's skin. The senses — taste, smell, hearing, sight, touch — are all developing in their own dedicated brain regions.

Dizziness when standing can persist — rise slowly and keep snacks nearby.
Your skin may itch as it stretches; fragrance-free moisturizer is your daily friend.
If leg cramps wake you at night, gentle calf stretches before bed help many people.
A pregnancy pillow stops being a luxury around now — side sleeping is a long game.
partnerTips: Keep your hand on the bump in the evenings; in a few weeks you'll feel what she feels.
Learn what the first kicks feel like for her so you can ask good questions.
Keep evenings unhurried; her body is on a construction schedule that never pauses.
Research car seats casually now — the options are vast and early browsing is free.
If she's anxious about feeling the baby 'enough,' remind her there's a wide normal range.

headline: Halfway home
development: You're at the halfway mark. Your baby is swallowing regularly and producing meconium, the first bowel movement. Those first flutters may now feel like unmistakable kicks.
momTips: Your appetite may surge — keep protein-rich snacks handy so the hunger works for you.
Anatomy scan week for many — ask all your questions; no question is too small.
Your belly button may start its slow migration; totally normal, usually temporary.
Sleep on your side now if you aren't already — a pillow between the knees keeps hips happy.
If hands feel puffy by evening, rings may want to move to a necklace chain.

Write the baby a letter at the halfway mark; someday that page will be priceless.
Take the halfway photo yourself — same spot, same pose, every few weeks from now on.
Start the conversation about parental leave logistics before calendars get tight.
Cook the celebratory dinner; halfway deserves more than takeout.

headline: Tasting dinner
development: Your baby swallows amniotic fluid flavored by what you eat — an early education in the family menu. The bone marrow has taken over blood cell production from the liver and spleen.

Keep calcium coming — bones are being built around the clock now.

Feel for kicks in the evening — this is often when they're findable from the outside.
Start assembling a shortlist of pediatricians; the good ones book out.
Ask her what she's craving this week and make it appear.

headline: Lips and eyebrows
development: Your baby's lips and eyebrows are distinct now, and the eyes are fully formed though the irises still lack color. Tiny tooth buds for adult teeth are in place.
momTips: Moisturize your belly daily — it may not prevent stretch marks, but it soothes the itch of stretching skin.

If your belly itches, moisturize after showering while the skin is still damp.

Defend her rest like it's your job — because it is.
If strangers' comments bother her, be ready to run interference with a smile.
Learn the Braxton Hicks vs. real contraction distinction; it prevents 2am panic later.
Take the bump photo this week yourself, and tell her why you love it.

development: Your baby can hear sounds from outside the womb and may startle or move to loud noises and music. The lungs are practicing breathing motions with amniotic fluid.

Swelling in feet by day's end is common; put them up when you can and mention sudden swelling to your provider.
If sleep is fragmenting, a wind-down routine — dim lights, no screens — genuinely helps.
Your baby can hear you now — narrate your day out loud sometimes.

Make the bedroom cooler and darker; her sleep quality is a shared project now.
Elevate her feet with a cushion when you're watching something together.
Keep a bottle of water filled and within her reach at all times — small thing, big effect.

headline: Hands that grasp

Take over one evening routine entirely — bath, tea, bed — so she can simply arrive.

Plan the third-trimester logistics now: who drives, who calls whom, what's the backup.

headline: Snug as a seed

momTips: Appointments likely move to every two weeks now — keep a running list of questions on your phone.
If baby's movements change pattern noticeably, call your provider — trust your sense of your baby.
Group B strep screening usually happens around now; it's a quick, routine swab.
Walking the stairs slowly is enough cardio; this is the season of gentle.
Practice the 'it's time' conversation: who drives, who you call, which door you leave from.
partnerTips: Add your own questions to her list too; you're allowed to be curious and prepared.
You're a participant, not a passenger — bring your own questions to the next appointment.
Learn the real signs of labor — water breaking, regular contractions — versus the false alarms.
Keep the hospital bag by the door from this week on.
Clear your calendar of anything non-essential after week 37.

headline: The long wiggle down
development: Your baby may begin descending into the pelvis, which can ease your heartburn and sharpen the pressure below. The downy lanugo hair is mostly gone.
momTips: Walking, bouncing on a birth ball, and rest in equal measure — listen to which one your body asks for.
If pressure low in the pelvis arrives, baby may be dropping — breathing gets easier, bathroom trips increase.
Weekly appointments usually begin now; bring your questions written down.
Rest in the afternoon if nights are broken; sleep is arriving in shifts.
Warm compresses on the lower back ease the new pelvic heaviness.
partnerTips: Install the car seat this week and get it inspected; it's the one task with no extension.
Check the car seat install with the manual in hand, then get it checked professionally.
Drive the hospital route at the actual hour you might need to.
Keep your boots by the door and your ringer on.
Ask her, weekly now: what can I take off your plate today?

headline: Early term, full wonder
development: Your baby is considered early term. The lungs and brain are still fine-tuning, and your baby is practicing breathing, sucking, and gripping all at once.
momTips: Wash the tiny clothes, pack the bag, then let yourself do nothing at all — you've earned the pause.
If you feel a gush or steady trickle of fluid, call your provider — that could be your water.
Losing the mucus plug can happen days before labor; note it, mention it, don't panic.
Contractions that fade when you rest are practice; ones that build are the real thing.
Let people help you now; accepting casseroles is a life skill.
partnerTips: Keep your phone charged and your calendar flexible from here on out.
Charge the camera, clear the memory card, know where the charger lives.
Write down the call tree: family, work, the friend taking the dog.
Keep the tank full and the seats clear; departure could be any evening.
Do a trial run of the middle-of-the-night exit, minus the drama.

headline: Waiting, beautifully
development: Your baby's brain and nervous system are still adding connections — development continues right up to birth. The grasp reflex is strong, and the eyes may be gray-blue for now.
momTips: Note the difference between practice contractions and the real thing: real ones get longer, stronger, and closer together.
Time any contractions: real labor gets longer, stronger, and closer together.
Sleep whenever sleep is available; labor doesn't schedule around your rest.
If anxiety spikes, slow breathing — in for four, out for six — genuinely steadies the nervous system.
Eat small, easy meals; your stomach has very little real estate left.
partnerTips: Agree on the 'it's time' plan: who you call first, which route you drive, what's in the bag by the door.
Rehearse the plan out loud once: route, calls, bag, door code.
Take over all household operations silently; she has one job now.
Keep snacks packed for yourself too — labor is long for everyone.
Tell her, plainly, that she's got this. Repeat as needed.

headline: Full term, full heart
development: Your baby is full term. The lungs are coated in surfactant, ready for that first breath, and fat continues to build for warmth in the outside world.
momTips: Do one thing this week that's purely for you — a slow breakfast, a favorite film, a long bath while you still can.
Any cramping, backache, or restlessness could be early labor — note patterns, stay hydrated, call with questions.
Walking and rest, alternating, is the classic final-week rhythm.
If your due date passes quietly, that's the norm, not a failure — most babies pick their own day.
Let the house be imperfect; you're about to do something enormous.
partnerTips: Keep showing up in small ways: water refilled, phone charged, shoulders rubbed. Presence is the job now.
Keep meals simple and her favorites available; appetite and queasiness can both visit this week.
Be reachable instantly — this is the week your phone stays loud.
If she's restless at midnight, walk the hallway with her, slowly, without checking your watch.
Prepare one true sentence for the delivery room — something she can hold onto.

headline: Any day, any hour
development: Your baby is fully developed and simply waiting for the right moment. The skull bones remain soft and slightly overlapping, designed for the journey to you.
momTips: Due dates are estimates — most babies arrive within a window on either side, and yours is no exception.
Your provider will discuss monitoring or induction timelines if you pass your date — ask all your questions.
Every cramp is not labor; every quiet day is not a problem. Call when unsure — that's what they're there for.
Sleep, eat, walk, repeat. The simplest routine is the right one now.
Look around at the quiet once in a while; it's the last of its kind.
partnerTips: Be her calm. Bring the snacks, make the calls, hold her hand, and get ready to meet your baby.
Take over every call, text, and 'any news?' inquiry — shield her from the waiting crowd.
Keep the fridge stocked with labor-friendly snacks and the freezer with post-birth meals.
If the days stretch past the due date, keep her spirits up with small, gentle plans.
Breathe with her. Practice now so it comes naturally when it counts.
